explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, says, "Let my teaching fall like rain and my speech settle like dew…" (Deuteronomy 32:2). He adds that it's like "gentle rain on new grass." Nothing loud or pushy about it. I wish my alarm clock had that kind of manners.

Moses does pick things that come down from the sky, so you're in the right neighborhood. But the song says rain and dew, and it says "gentle rain on new grass, like showers on tender plants" (Deuteronomy 32:2). Snow and frost never make the list. Moses is staying with the softer, wetter stuff.

Moses isn't going for loud and dramatic here, friend. He says his teaching should fall like rain and settle like dew (Deuteronomy 32:2). Those are some of the quietest things you can get from the sky. Wind and fire are not on his list.

Moses sings, "He is the Rock, His work is perfect; all His ways are just." (Deuteronomy 32:4). A rock holds still when everything else is shaking. I like a name like that, because it tells me where to stand.
A tower is tall and sturdy, so I see why you reached for it. But the song's word is Rock. "He is the Rock, His work is perfect…" (Deuteronomy 32:4). Moses doesn't call Him a tower here.

A mountain is big and it stays put, so that's a fair guess, friend. But Moses uses a different word. He says, "He is the Rock, His work is perfect…" (Deuteronomy 32:4). Same solid feeling, just a smaller word.

Moses asks, "Is He not your Father and Creator? Has He not made you and established you?" (Deuteronomy 32:6). Two big titles in one breath. He's asking whether this is how you repay the One who made you.

Friend and neighbor are warm words, but they aren't the ones Moses uses. He asks, "Is He not your Father and Creator?" (Deuteronomy 32:6). That's a much bigger claim than a neighbor. A neighbor didn't make you.

Partner and ally sound like a business deal, friend. The song says something much deeper. Moses asks, "Is He not your Father and Creator? Has He not made you and established you?" (Deuteronomy 32:6). He made them.

Moses sings, "But the LORD's portion is His people, Jacob His allotted inheritance." (Deuteronomy 32:9). Out of everything the Most High could have called His own, the song names His people. That's a good line to hear.

This one is true, friend. The song says, "But the LORD's portion is His people, Jacob His allotted inheritance." (Deuteronomy 32:9). The portion is His people, and the song names Jacob. That's the statement on the card.

Moses sings, "He found him in a desert land, in a barren, howling wilderness…" (Deuteronomy 32:10). Barren and howling, and still the LORD found him there. The song says the LORD surrounded him, instructed him and guarded him.

Nineveh isn't in this song at all. Moses sings that the LORD "found him in a desert land, in a barren, howling wilderness" (Deuteronomy 32:10). No city anywhere. It's wide open desert with some howling.
Hebron doesn't show up in this song, friend. Moses says, "He found him in a desert land, in a barren, howling wilderness…" (Deuteronomy 32:10). Nothing about a valley. Just desert and howling.

Moses sings, "As an eagle stirs up its nest and hovers over its young, He spread His wings to catch them and carried them on His pinions." (Deuteronomy 32:11). Catch them, then carry them. That's a lot of care packed into one picture.

A net would catch something, sure. But the song says the LORD spread His wings, like an eagle hovering over its young (Deuteronomy 32:11). Then He "carried them on His pinions." It's wings all the way down.

Arms would work for a person, but Moses is painting a bird. The song says, "He spread His wings to catch them and carried them on His pinions." (Deuteronomy 32:11). The eagle picture stays an eagle picture.
The song says the opposite. "The LORD alone led him, and no foreign god was with him." (Deuteronomy 32:12). Alone. No helpers on that list. It was just Him.

Moses sings, "The LORD alone led him, and no foreign god was with him." (Deuteronomy 32:12). No foreign god was there, let alone helping. I've seen a whole kitchen crowd at one batch, and this is nothing like that. The LORD led His people by Himself.

Plain and simple is not how the song tells it, friend. Moses sings of curds, milk, lambs, "the choicest grains of wheat," and "the juice of the finest grapes" (Deuteronomy 32:14). Choicest and finest are not plain words. Even I'd stop mid-stamp for a list like that.

Right, because the song doesn't call it plain. Moses sings of "the choicest grains of wheat" and says, "From the juice of the finest grapes you drank the wine." (Deuteronomy 32:14). That's the good stuff, the choicest and the finest. It makes my best cookie dough look humble.

The song says, "He abandoned the God who made him and scorned the Rock of his salvation." (Deuteronomy 32:15). Jeshurun is full and comfortable, and he walks away from the One who made him. I think a full stomach can make a short memory.

I wish the song went that way, friend. It says Jeshurun "abandoned the God who made him and scorned the Rock of his salvation." (Deuteronomy 32:15). No thank-you note in that verse. It goes the other direction.

Following would have been the good ending, but that's not what the song says. Jeshurun "abandoned the God who made him and scorned the Rock of his salvation." (Deuteronomy 32:15). He walked away instead of following.

Moses sings, "They sacrificed to demons, not to God, to gods they had not known…" (Deuteronomy 32:17). Gods they had not known. They gave offerings to something that never knew them either. That's a heavy part of the song.

Angels show up later in the song, but on the good side. Moses sings that all God's angels should worship Him (Deuteronomy 32:43). Here, the verse says, "They sacrificed to demons, not to God…" (Deuteronomy 32:17). Those are different beings.
Stars are my favorite thing in the sky, so I'd love to blame them, friend. But the song doesn't say stars. It says, "They sacrificed to demons, not to God…" (Deuteronomy 32:17).

Not old at all, friend. The song calls them "newly arrived gods, which your fathers did not fear." (Deuteronomy 32:17). These gods were new and their fathers hadn't feared them. No ancient history there.
Moses sings about "gods they had not known, to newly arrived gods, which your fathers did not fear." (Deuteronomy 32:17). New arrivals, not old gods. Even the fathers hadn't feared them.

The song says, "When the LORD saw this, He rejected them, provoked to anger by His sons and daughters." (Deuteronomy 32:19). It's His own people who provoked Him. I think that hurts more than a stranger doing it.
The kings aren't named here, friend. The verse says the LORD was "provoked to anger by His sons and daughters." (Deuteronomy 32:19). Those are His own people.
No armies are in this verse. It says He was "provoked to anger by His sons and daughters." (Deuteronomy 32:19). It's His own people that the song points to, not Egypt.
God says, "I will hide My face from them; I will see what will be their end." (Deuteronomy 32:20). This is a heavy line, and I'm not going to joke on it. I think it's a hard thing to hear.
The song says He will, friend. God says, "I will hide My face from them; I will see what will be their end." (Deuteronomy 32:20). It's a heavy line. This one deserves a quiet moment.

explanations.answer: By those who aren't even a people
explanations.explanation: God says, "So I will make them jealous by those who are not a people; I will make them angry by a nation without understanding." (Deuteronomy 32:21). They made Him jealous with what is not God, and He answers in kind. Not a people at all.

explanations.answer: By those who lead His own people
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention leaders. God says, "I will make them jealous by those who are not a people…" (Deuteronomy 32:21). It's about those who aren't a people, not those who lead His own.

explanations.answer: By those who serve at His altar
explanations.explanation: Nobody at the altar is named here, friend. God says, "I will make them jealous by those who are not a people; I will make them angry by a nation without understanding." (Deuteronomy 32:21).

explanations.answer: Their enemies would take the credit
explanations.explanation: God says He would have gone further "if I had not dreaded the taunt of the enemy, lest their adversaries misunderstand and say: 'Our own hand has prevailed; it was not the LORD who did all this.'" (Deuteronomy 32:27). It's about what the enemies would say. They'd take the credit that belongs to Him.

explanations.answer: Moses would beg Him to stop
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't beg in this song, friend. The reason in the text is that God dreaded "the taunt of the enemy, lest their adversaries misunderstand" (Deuteronomy 32:27). They would say, 'Our own hand has prevailed.'

explanations.answer: Israel would turn back to Him
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't say that is what held Him back. The text says it was because He dreaded "the taunt of the enemy, lest their adversaries misunderstand and say: 'Our own hand has prevailed…'" (Deuteronomy 32:27). It's about the enemies and what they'd say.

explanations.answer: The LORD had given them up
explanations.explanation: Moses asks, "How could one man pursue a thousand, or two put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them, unless the LORD had given them up?" (Deuteronomy 32:30). Those numbers don't happen on their own. According to the song, that's the only way it could.

explanations.answer: Their army had grown too small
explanations.explanation: A small army makes sense as a guess, friend. But the song doesn't say that. It says it could only happen "unless their Rock had sold them, unless the LORD had given them up" (Deuteronomy 32:30).

explanations.answer: Their weapons had grown too old
explanations.explanation: Old weapons would be a fair guess. But the song gives a different reason. One chasing a thousand happens only "unless their Rock had sold them, unless the LORD had given them up" (Deuteronomy 32:30).
The song says, "Their grapes are poisonous; their clusters are bitter." (Deuteronomy 32:32). The vine is from Sodom and Gomorrah, and the fruit matches. You wouldn't want a taste of that.
Sweet is the opposite of what the song says, friend. The verse says, "Their grapes are poisonous; their clusters are bitter." (Deuteronomy 32:32). No sweetness in that vineyard.
Unripe grapes would just be sour. But the song goes further. It says, "Their grapes are poisonous; their clusters are bitter." (Deuteronomy 32:32). Poisonous is a much bigger problem than unripe.
The song puts vengeance in a different set of hands. God says, "Vengeance is Mine; I will repay." (Deuteronomy 32:35). It belongs to Him. Not to His people.
God says, "Vengeance is Mine; I will repay." (Deuteronomy 32:35). It belongs to Him, not to His people. That's the statement the song makes.

explanations.answer: When He sees their strength is gone
explanations.explanation: The song says the LORD "will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants when He sees that their strength is gone and no one remains, slave or free." (Deuteronomy 32:36). It comes when their strength is gone. The song turns toward hope here.

explanations.answer: When they win their next battle
explanations.explanation: Winning isn't what the song says. It says compassion comes "when He sees that their strength is gone and no one remains, slave or free." (Deuteronomy 32:36). It's when their strength is gone, not when they win.

explanations.answer: When they bring a bigger offering
explanations.explanation: No bigger offering in this verse, friend. The song says He will have compassion "when He sees that their strength is gone and no one remains, slave or free." (Deuteronomy 32:36). It comes when their strength is gone.
God says, "See now that I am He; there is no God besides Me." (Deuteronomy 32:39). There is no other. That settles every question.
This one is true. God says, "See now that I am He; there is no God besides Me." (Deuteronomy 32:39). He says there is no other God. The song says it plainly.
God says, "I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal, and there is no one who can deliver from My hand." (Deuteronomy 32:39). No one. That includes everything on this card.
A king would be a big name, but the verse says nobody. God says, "…there is no one who can deliver from My hand." (Deuteronomy 32:39). Not even a king.

Angels do appear in the song, friend, but only to worship Him. "Let all God's angels worship Him," it says (Deuteronomy 32:43). They don't deliver anyone from His hand. God says, "…there is no one who can deliver from My hand." (Deuteronomy 32:39).
God says, "For I lift up My hand to heaven and declare: As surely as I live forever…" (Deuteronomy 32:40). His promise is as sure as His own life. It can't get more solid than that.
The heavens are a big comparison, but the song doesn't use them here. God says, "As surely as I live forever…" (Deuteronomy 32:40). He swears by His own life.
Mountains are strong, friend, but they aren't the comparison here. God says, "As surely as I live forever…" (Deuteronomy 32:40). He swears by His own life.

Moses sings, "Rejoice, O nations, with His people…" (Deuteronomy 32:43). The call goes out beyond Israel. A song that began by calling the heavens and the earth to listen ends by calling the nations to rejoice.
Priests aren't named in the closing call, friend. It says, "Rejoice, O nations, with His people…" (Deuteronomy 32:43). The nations are the ones called to rejoice.

Elders show up earlier in the song, where Moses says to ask your elders and they will inform you (Deuteronomy 32:7). But the closing call is different. It says, "Rejoice, O nations, with His people…" (Deuteronomy 32:43).
